blocks.text: Mary Magdalene, the other Mary, and the women who followed Jesus are not incidental spectators. Matthew places them at Jesus’ death and burial, beginning a continuous witness role that also extends to the empty tomb, the angelic announcement, and the risen Jesus’ commission to tell the brothers.

Matthew surrounds Jesus’ death with darkness, the tearing of the temple curtain, an earthquake, opened tombs, raised saints, and the centurion’s confession. These extraordinary signs make the death scene larger than the execution itself within Matthew’s narration. The later account of priests securing the tomb is also distinctive to Matthew and introduces the dispute over a claim that the disciples stole Jesus’ body.

The actions and words surrounding the crucifixion in verses 35–46 may be read as part of a broader New Testament practice of quoting and echoing psalms when presenting Jesus’ suffering. New Testament authors also employ psalms in discussions of resurrection, enthronement, priesthood, mission, worship, creation rule, and believing communities, though interpretations of particular echoes can be disputed.

Matthew assigns narrative agency to several Judean and Roman actors rather than to one undifferentiated group. At the same time, crucifixion remains a Roman state execution, framed by provincial authority and elite power. Holding both features together keeps the chapter’s distribution of responsibility from obscuring the political power that carried out the sentence.
